INDEPENDENT SERVICE AUDITOR’S REPORT
To MongoDB, Inc.:
Scope
We have examined MongoDB, Inc.’s (“MongoDB” or the “service organization”) accompanying description of its
MongoDB Cloud Service Platform system, in Section 3, throughout the period October 1, 2024, to March 31, 2025,
(the “description”), based on the criteria for a description of a service organization’s system in DC section 200, 2018
Description Criteria for a Description of a Service Organization’s System in a SOC 2® Report (AICPA, Description
Criteria) (“description criteria”), and the suitability of the design and operating effectiveness of controls stated in the
description throughout the period October 1, 2024, to March 31, 2025, to provide reasonable assurance that
MongoDB’s service commitments and system requirements were achieved based on the trust services criteria
relevant to security, availability, and confidentiality (“applicable trust services criteria”) set forth in TSP section 100,
Trust Services Criteria for Security, Availability, Processing Integrity, Confidentiality, and Privacy (AICPA, Trust
Services Criteria). We have also examined the suitability of the design and operating effectiveness of controls to
meet the applicable requirements set forth in version 9.6 of the HITRUST CSF (“HITRUST CSF criteria”) throughout
the period October 1, 2024, to March 31, 2025.
MongoDB uses various subservice organizations for cloud hosting services. The description indicates that
complementary subservice organization controls that are suitably designed and operating effectively are necessary,
along with controls at MongoDB, to achieve the HITRUST CSF criteria and MongoDB’s service commitments and
system requirements based on the applicable trust services criteria. The description presents MongoDB’s controls,
the applicable trust services criteria and HITRUST CSF criteria, and the types of complementary subservice
organization controls assumed in the design of MongoDB’s controls. The description does not disclose the actual
controls at the subservice organizations. Our examination did not include the services provided by the subservice
organizations, and we have not evaluated the suitability of the design or operating effectiveness of such
complementary subservice organization controls.
Service Organization’s Responsibilities
MongoDB is responsible for its service commitments and system requirements and for designing, implementing,
and operating effective controls within the system to provide reasonable assurance that MongoDB’s service
commitments and system requirements, and HITRUST CSF criteria were achieved. MongoDB has provided the
accompanying assertion, in Section 2, (“assertion”) about the description and the suitability of design and operating
effectiveness of controls stated therein. MongoDB is also responsible for preparing the description and assertion,
including the completeness, accuracy, and method of presentation of the description and assertion; providing the
services covered by the description; selecting the applicable trust services criteria and HITRUST CSF criteria and
stating the related controls in the description; and identifying the risks that threaten the achievement of the service
organization’s service commitments and system requirements.
MongoDB is also responsible for selecting the HITRUST CSF criteria as additional criteria and implementing
controls to meet the requirements set forth in the HITRUST CSF criteria.
Service Auditor’s Responsibilities
Our responsibility is to express an opinion on the description and on the suitability of design and operating
effectiveness of controls stated in the description based on our examination. Our examination was conducted in
accordance with attestation standards established by the American Institute of Certified Public Accountants (AICPA)
and in accordance with International Standard on Assurance Engagements 3000 (Revised), Assurance
Engagements Other Than Audits or Reviews of Historical Financial Information, issued by the International Auditing
and Assurance Standards Board. Those standards require that we plan and perform our examination to obtain
reasonable assurance about whether, in all material respects, the description is presented in accordance with the
description criteria and the controls stated therein were suitably designed and operated effectively to provide
reasonable assurance that the HITRUST CSF criteria were achieved and the service organization’s service
2

commitments and system requirements were achieved based on the applicable trust services criteria. We believe
that the evidence we obtained is sufficient and appropriate to provide a reasonable basis for our opinion.
An examination of the description of a service organization’s system and the suitability of the design and operating
effectiveness of controls involves the following:
•

Obtaining an understanding of the system and the service organization’s service commitments and system
requirements.

•

Assessing the risks that the description is not presented in accordance with the description criteria and that
controls were not suitably designed or did not operate effectively.

•

Performing procedures to obtain evidence about whether the description is presented in accordance with
the description criteria.

•

Performing procedures to obtain evidence about whether controls stated in the description were suitably
designed to provide reasonable assurance that the service organization achieved the applicable HITRUST
CSF criteria and its service commitments and system requirements based on the applicable trust services
criteria.

•

Testing the operating effectiveness of controls stated in the description to provide reasonable assurance
that the service organization achieved the HITRUST CSF criteria and its service commitments and system
requirements based on the applicable trust services criteria.

•

Evaluating the overall presentation of the description.

Our examination also included performing such other procedures as we considered necessary in the circumstances.
Service Auditor’s Independence and Quality Control
We are required to be independent and to meet our other ethical responsibilities in accordance with relevant ethical
requirements relating to the engagement, including the Code of Professional Conduct established by the AICPA
and the International Ethics Standards Board for Accountants’ Code of Ethics for Professional Accountants.
We applied the Statements on Quality Control Standards established by the AICPA and, accordingly, maintain a
comprehensive system of quality control.
Inherent Limitations
The description is prepared to meet the common needs of a broad range of report users and may not, therefore,
include every aspect of the system that individual users may consider important to meet their informational needs.
There are inherent limitations in the effectiveness of any system of internal control, including the possibility of human
error and the circumvention of controls.
Because of their nature, controls may not always operate effectively to provide reasonable assurance that the
HITRUST CSF criteria are achieved or the service organization’s service commitments and system requirements
are achieved based on the applicable trust services criteria. Also, the projection to the future of any conclusions
about the suitability of the design and operating effectiveness of controls is subject to the risk that controls may
become inadequate because of changes in conditions or that the degree of compliance with the policies or
procedures may deteriorate.
Description of Test of Controls
The specific controls we tested, and the nature, timing, and results of those tests are presented in Section 4 of our
report titled “Testing Matrices.”
Opinion
In our opinion, in all material respects:
•

the description presents the MongoDB Cloud Service Platform system that was designed and implemented
throughout the period October 1, 2024, to March 31, 2025, in accordance with the description criteria;

and business partners, prospective user entities and business partners, and regulators who have sufficient
knowledge and understanding of the following:

how the service organization’s system interacts with user entities, business partners, subservice

MANAGEMENT’S ASSERTION
We have prepared the accompanying description of the MongoDB Cloud Service Platform system, in Section 3,
throughout the period October 1, 2024, to March 31, 2025, (the “description”) based on the criteria for a description
of a service organization’s system in DC section 200, 2018 Description Criteria for a Description of a Service
Organization’s System in a SOC 2® Report (AICPA, Description Criteria), (“description criteria”). The description is
intended to provide report users with information about the MongoDB Cloud Service Platform system that may be
useful when assessing the risks arising from interactions with MongoDB’s system, particularly information about
system controls that MongoDB has designed, implemented, and operated to provide reasonable assurance that the
criteria set forth in applicable requirements set forth in version 9.6 of the HITRUST CSF (“HITRUST CSF criteria”)
were achieved and MongoDB’s service commitments and system requirements were achieved based on the trust
services criteria relevant to security, availability, and confidentiality (“applicable trust services criteria”) set forth in
TSP section 100, Trust Services Criteria for Security, Availability, Processing Integrity, Confidentiality, and Privacy
(AICPA, Trust Services Criteria).
MongoDB uses various subservice organizations for cloud hosting services. The description indicates that
complementary subservice organization controls that are suitably designed and operating effectively are necessary,
along with controls at MongoDB, to achieve the HITRUST CSF criteria and the MongoDB’s service commitments
and system requirements based on the applicable trust services criteria. The description presents MongoDB’s
controls, the applicable trust services criteria and HITRUST CSF criteria, and the types of complementary
subservice organization controls assumed in the design of MongoDB’s controls. The description does not disclose
the actual controls at the subservice organizations.
We confirm, to the best of our knowledge and belief, that:
•

the description presents the MongoDB Cloud Service Platform system that was designed and implemented
throughout the period October 1, 2024, to March 31, 2025, in accordance with the description criteria;

•

the controls stated in the description were suitably designed throughout the period October 1, 2024, to
March 31, 2025, to provide reasonable assurance that the HITRUST CSF criteria would be met and the
MongoDB’s service commitments and system requirements would be achieved based on the applicable
trust services criteria, if its controls operated effectively throughout that period, and if the subservice
organizations and applied the complementary controls assumed in the design of MongoDB’s controls
throughout that period; and

•

the controls stated in the description operated effectively throughout the period October 1, 2024, to March
31, 2025, to provide reasonable assurance that the HITRUST CSF criteria were achieved and the
MongoDB’s service commitments and system requirements were achieved based on the applicable trust
services criteria if complementary subservice organization controls assumed in the design of MongoDB’s
controls operated effectively throughout that period.

OVERVIEW OF OPERATIONS
Company Background
MongoDB, Inc. (MongoDB) was first established in 2007 as a software company called “10gen”. MongoDB (then
“10gen”) shifted focus to its database as the primary product after noticing a gap when building its platform. The
company name was later changed to match the database product they went on to create, called MongoDB.
MongoDB develops and provides commercial support for the open-source database MongoDB, a NoSQL database
that stores data in JavaScript Object Notation (JSON)-like documents with flexible schema. Headquartered in New
York, New York, MongoDB has employees in 29 countries with over 4,537 employees worldwide. MongoDB
provides a suite of services and products. Current customers of MongoDB include over one-third of Fortune 100
and various businesses across Europe, Middle East, and Africa (EMEA) and Asia Pacific.
Description of Services Provided
The MongoDB Cloud Services Platform comprises in-scope cloud products which include MongoDB Atlas,
MongoDB Atlas for Government, Atlas App Services, Realm, MongoDB Charts, Atlas Data Federation, MongoDB
Atlas Serverless Database, MongoDB Cloud Manager, and Online Archive.
MongoDB Atlas is a cloud-hosted Database-as-a-Service (DaaS) product that is available on-demand. MongoDB
Atlas enables users to set up, operate, and scale a MongoDB deployment in the cloud; therefore, allowing
developers to focus on their core development while leaving database operations such as scaling, security, high
availability, and other operations to be managed by MongoDB. MongoDB Atlas is available within the Amazon Web
Services (AWS), Google Cloud Platform (GCP) and Microsoft Azure (Azure) cloud platforms. Additionally, users
can choose from up to over 95+ cloud regions to host their databases (Northeast, West, Southeast, Canada, etc.).
Storage volumes are configured to be encrypted on AWS, GCP, and Azure by default. Additionally, each MongoDB
Atlas group is provisioned into its own virtual private cloud (VPC), which isolates data from other MongoDB Atlas
users.
Enterprise security features can be enabled for MongoDB Atlas clusters, which include the following:
•

Database-level auditing: For regulatory compliance, security administrators can use MongoDB Atlas to
retrieve audit logs tracking data manipulation language (DML), data definition language (DDL), and data
control language (DCL) operations taken against a managed cluster.

•

Lightweight directory access protocol (LDAP) integration: Atlas offers integration with customer LDAP
servers to help simplify access control and granular permissions management for users and applications.

•

Bring your own key management service: Atlas supports the encrypted storage engine, a native encryption
option for WiredTiger. With this option enabled, database files are written to the filesystem, encrypted, and
customers maintain control over the encryption keys for their managed clusters. To use this option,
customers may bring their own encryption key with AWS or GCP Key Management Service (KMS) or Azure
Key Vault (KV).

•

Online archive configuration: Atlas offers MongoDB Online Archive to configure data in a collection to be
archived by specifying an archiving rule. Once the Online Archive is configured on the cluster, Atlas creates
two federated database instances on the cluster for the archive only and for the cluster and archive. The
online archive is configurable through Atlas command line interface (CLI), API, and user interface.

MongoDB Atlas support ensures that database clusters are running and configured properly.
encountered within the MongoDB Atlas, community support is available.

If bugs are

MongoDB Atlas for Government (A4G) is a fully-managed cloud database for the U.S. government (federal
agencies, state agencies, and cloud service providers who process or store federal data. A4G is distinct from
commercial MongoDB Atlas, it supports a subset of the commercial MongoDB Atlas features and is deployed and
managed in a completely separate environment. The Atlas developer data platform is an integrated set of data and
application services that supports transactional workloads, time series data, search, and petabyte data storage.
8
This document was distributed using Conveyor, a secure customer trust management platform. For information about how
you can start using Conveyor for free to build trust with your customers, visit www.conveyor.com.

Atlas App Services, Realm is a serverless Backend as a Service (BaaS) platform which is built on top of Atlas to
provide automatic integration to databases without the need to deploy a database backend to store the customers
application data. The Atlas App Services, Realm platform is a combination of NoSQL based server and client
components connected via sync protocol to enable real-time, connected apps and services. The Atlas App
Services, Realm platform has two major components: the Realm Database object-oriented, cross-platform
database that persists data locally on device; and the Realm Object Server which functions as a middleware
component in the mobile app architecture and manages data synchronization, event handling, and integration with
legacy systems.
MongoDB Charts is a modern data visualization tool that allows users to connect to their Atlas collections as a data
source, create charts and graphs, build dashboards, and share them with other users for collaboration. Users can
also embed charts in their own web sites and apps. Built for the document model, Charts handles complex data
structures natively: nested documents, arrays, and more.
Atlas Data Federation is a serverless, scalable query service which allows customers to natively query and analyze
data across AWS Simple Storage Service (S3) and MongoDB Atlas. Atlas Data Federation deploys multiple
compute nodes to process queries against the target data. Atlas Data Federation is a multi-tenant on-demand
query processing engine that allows customers to utilize the MongoDB Query Language (MQL) on cloud object
store data in multiple formats including JSON, BSON, CSV, TSV, Avro, ORC, and Parquet.
MongoDB Atlas Serverless Database is a cloud-based service offering non-dedicated tiers to support elastic scaling
and consumption-based pricing for customers. Serverless databases are an expansion of the serverless model
beyond the application layer where serverless architecture is more common. With the traditional DBaaS, the
database is fully managed for customers and deployed as a specific pre-provisioned instance size with a specific
price. A serverless architecture for a cloud database means that customers do not select an instance size instead
the customer sets up a database and it grows as necessary with data size and throughput and the cost scales
accordingly. MongoDB Atlas Serverless allows customers to deploy a serverless database via serverless instances.
MongoDB Atlas Serverless provides similar features as the MongoDB Atlas cloud product with important
distinctions, MongoDB Atlas Serverless is available for its serverless applications with low or variable traffic.
Minimal configuration is required for this service. Customers choose their cloud region during the initial sign up and
the database will dynamically scale to meet the demand of their workload.
MongoDB Cloud Manager is a cloud-based management platform that enables customers to deploy, monitor, back
up, and scale MongoDB deployments in one platform. Cloud Manager can automate, monitor, and back up the
customers MongoDB infrastructure. Automation within Cloud Manager enables customers to configure, maintain,
deploy and upgrade new or existing MongoDB nodes and clusters. Cloud Manager monitoring provides real-time
reporting, visualization, and alerting on key database and hardware indicators. The monitoring capabilities include
collecting statistics from the nodes in the MongoDB deployment and transmitting database statistics back to Cloud
Manager to report deployment status in real time. Through Cloud Manager a customer can view historic data to
create operational baselines and support capacity planning as well as monitor real-time performance for load spikes,
hot collections, and slow queries. Cloud Manager backup capabilities include scheduled snapshots and point-intime recovery of the MongoDB replica sets and sharded clusters. Cloud Manager helps enable database
management by handling administration tasks through automation.

PRINCIPAL SERVICE COMMITMENTS AND SYSTEM REQUIREMENTS
MongoDB designs its processes and procedures related to the MongoDB Cloud Services Platform to meet its
objectives for its Cloud Services Platform. Those objectives are based on the service commitments that MongoDB
makes to user entities, the laws and regulations that govern the provision of the MongoDB Cloud Services Platform,
and the financial, operational, and compliance requirements that MongoDB has established for the services.
MongoDB is committed to providing their customers with a secure environment with which to conduct their business
as pertains to the use of the MongoDB Cloud Services Platform. The commitment to security begins with the
contract signed between MongoDB and the customer. The contract contains specific language around the security
that MongoDB will provide as part of their ongoing service, including industry standard data security and data
9
This document was distributed using Conveyor, a secure customer trust management platform. For information about how
you can start using Conveyor for free to build trust with your customers, visit www.conveyor.com.

protection practices as outlined in their Technical and Organizational Security measures linked within the standard
terms of service. MongoDB also commits to utilizing system security precautions including, but not limited to,
encryption and firewall technology. In the event of a downgrade to security or an incident that may jeopardize their
security commitment, MongoDB has in place a security incident management procedure by which they identify,
investigate, and resolve the incident. MongoDB communicates security incidents to external users as deemed
necessary and based on the impact of the incident.
MongoDB’s availability commitments to user entities are documented and communicated in the Service Level
Agreements (SLAs) and other customer agreements, as well as in the description of the service offering provided
online. The principal availability commitments are standardized and include fully managed backups based on
customer preference, automatic failover of the MongoDB clusters across multiple availability zones within a region,
the performance of an annual business continuity plan test, and capacity management to help ensure the availability
of the MongoDB Cloud Services Platform.
MongoDB's confidentiality commitments are documented within customer contracts, non-disclosure agreements,
high security addendum business associate agreements and its published privacy notice. MongoDB’s
confidentiality commitments include retaining data subject to legal and/or regulatory requirements. MongoDB has
established a classification scheme to protect information according to risk levels. This framework allows MongoDB
to select appropriate security controls and balance protection needs with costs and business efficiencies. MongoDB
has defined how information is to be accessed, transmitted, and shared with third parties outside of MongoDB, and
retained. Customer data is encrypted at rest and retained until the end of the engagement. Upon completion of
the engagement, the customer is responsible for deleting their own data through the MongoDB portal.
In accordance with MongoDB’s assertion, and the description criteria, the aforementioned service commitments
and requirements are those principal service commitments and requirements common to the broad base of users
of the system and may therefore not fully address the specific service commitments and requirements made to all
system users, in each individual case.

COMPONENTS OF THE SYSTEM USED TO PROVIDE THE SERVICE
System Boundaries
A system is designed, implemented, and operated to achieve specific business objectives in accordance with
management-specified requirements. The purpose of the system description is to delineate the boundaries of the
system, which includes the services outlined above and the five components described below: infrastructure,
software, people, procedures, and data.
Infrastructure and Software
MongoDB uses a variety of infrastructure and software for its MongoDB Atlas, MongoDB Atlas for Government,
Atlas App Services, Realm, MongoDB Atlas Data Federation, MongoDB Charts, MongoDB Atlas Serverless
Database, and MongoDB Cloud Manager products that comprise the MongoDB Cloud Services Platform.
MongoDB, the MongoDB enterprise database, is configured to utilize authentication and encryption by default, both
for customer access and intra-node communication. MongoDB’s in-scope cloud products (i.e., Atlas, Atlas App
Services, Realm, Atlas Data Federation, Charts, Atlas Serverless Database, and Cloud Manager) are written in
Java, JavaScript and Go. Access to MongoDB’s in-scope products, is managed via the Atlas web user interface
(UI), is encrypted, and authenticated by the transport layer security (TLS) protocol over hyper-text transfer protocol
secure (HTTPS). Data sent to and from the MongoDB Cloud web UI is encrypted in transit. Data stored by
MongoDB Cloud Services Platform by default is configured for encryption-at-rest. Additionally, MongoDB offers
cloud infrastructure on AWS, GCP, and Azure to power MongoDB Cloud Services Platform customer virtual
machines. MongoDB Cloud Services Platform customers are provided with a dedicated virtual private cloud and
dedicated virtual machines that are deployed based on customer parameters.

10
This document was distributed using Conveyor, a secure customer trust management platform. For information about how
you can start using Conveyor for free to build trust with your customers, visit www.conveyor.com.

MongoDB’s Atlas control plane primary data centers are located in the US East Region but are not limited to just
the East Region. With regard to the customer data plane, based on customer needs for where their data should
reside, multiple locations are available worldwide via the underlying Infrastructure-as-a-Service Cloud Service
Providers (i.e., AWS, GCP, Azure) utilized by MongoDB Atlas. AWS, GCP, and Azure regions include, but are not
limited to, Virginia, California, Oregon, Ohio, Sydney, Ireland, Sao Paulo, Montreal, Singapore, Tokyo, Seoul,
Mumbai, London, Paris, Hong Kong, Bahrain, Cape Town, Toronto, and Frankfurt. AWS, GCP, and Azure regions
consist of multiple physical data centers, divided into availability zones, which are fully independent operating
environments (different physical plants, locations, power supplies, network connectivity, fault lines, etc.).
Application servers draw data from a variety of database servers and file servers, which are in turn protected by
firewalls (i.e., security groups) that are managed within the AWS, GCP, and Azure cloud platforms. The managed
firewalls segment traffic between types of servers are deny-by-default and allow only sourced traffic on specified
protocols to pass between server instances.
The in-scope MongoDB Cloud Services Platform products are developed and maintained by MongoDB Cloud
software engineers. The components of the in-scope MongoDB Cloud products are presented to customers through
a unified web application interface. Once authenticated, users are able to create new deployments in a
geographical region of their choice, configure database size, redundancy, and configure their database parameters.
MongoDB Cloud Services Platform also provides users the ability to monitor key aspects of their database as well
as automate database administration tasks such as database configuration, infrastructure provisioning, patches,
scaling events, and encrypted backups. Once a MongoDB Atlas database is created and configured, users then
configure their application to communicate with their MongoDB database directly. Additional mechanisms are in
place to automatically detect configuration drift should it occur in MongoDB Cloud production environments. The
MongoDB Cloud Security team runs network scans to help ensure that network security groups are behaving as
expected in the MongoDB Cloud Control Plane (CCP). Similarly, post-provisioning, the MongoDB Cloud
engineering team monitors customer cluster configurations on the Cloud Service Provider environments (i.e., AWS,
GCP, Azure) to identify and remediate any drift.

People
Personnel involved in the operation and use of the system are:
•

Executive management – Responsible for overseeing company-wide activities, establishing, and
accomplishing goals, and overseeing objectives.

•

Human resources (HR) – Responsible for HR policies, practices, and processes with a focus on key HR
department delivery areas (e.g., talent acquisitions, employee retention, compensation, employee benefits,
performance management, employee relations and training, and development).

•

Information security personnel – Responsible for information security risk management and identification,
monitoring, and compliance of security issues and incidents throughout the service delivery infrastructure.

•

Cloud engineering team – Responsible for development of in-scope MongoDB Cloud products and product
features, including front end development, back-end server development, client-side tool development,
infrastructure expansion and automation, security feature development, as well as testing, quality
assurance (QA) and staging.

•

Cloud security team – Responsible for managing, monitoring, and supporting information and systems from
unauthorized access and use while maintaining integrity and availability.

•

Site reliability engineers (SREs) / part of Cloud Engineering – Responsible for reliability, availability,
scalability, and deployment of MongoDB Cloud’s computing infrastructure.

Procedures
HR and Training
Job descriptions are documented and utilized to outline the required skills needed and the employee responsibilities
for the job. As part of the hiring process, employment candidates are interviewed for the required skillset of the job
position the employment candidate is applying for, and employment candidates must go through a background
check prior to being hired. Upon hire, employees are required to sign an acknowledgment of the receipt and
understanding of the employee handbook and information security policies as well as agreeing to follow MongoDB’s
policies and procedures. Additionally, an employee remedial procedure is documented within the employee
handbook and information security policies that outlines that employees may be disciplined up to termination for
non-compliance with MongoDB’s policies and procedures. As part of the on-boarding process, HR enters the new
hire into the HR system which grants the employee access to their HR account and e-mail. For additional access
requests to other MongoDB programs / platforms, either the employee or the employee’s manager will submit an
access request in the IAM system (Identity and Access Management) and the system owner will approve or deny
the request based on the employee’s position.
New hires are required to complete security awareness training to understand their responsibilities for security and
complying with MongoDB’s security policies and procedures. Training courses are available to new and existing
employees to maintain and advance the skill level.

12
This document was distributed using Conveyor, a secure customer trust management platform. For information about how
you can start using Conveyor for free to build trust with your customers, visit www.conveyor.com.

Access, Authentication, and Authorization
In-scope systems, including the in-scope application instances, databases, operating system, and firewalls are
configured to authenticate users via a unique user account and require either a username and password, multifactor authentication (MFA), or a secure shell (SSH) connection. Minimum password settings are enforced at
production environment layers. In order to access the production environment, users must first authenticate
remotely via SSH.
Authorized internal users requiring remote privileged access to the in-scope systems are required to authenticate
via an encrypted VPN in order to first obtain an office Internet Protocol (IP) address. Accounts and configurations
within the centralized identity management tool integrate with the VPN via the Layer Two Tunneling Protocol (L2TP)
over IPsec protocol – a client/server protocol that runs on the application layer and provides a centralized
understanding between the Okta server and VPN with the centralized identity management tool usernames and
passwords. Additionally, Okta is utilized as a single sign on tool.
For further access to the in-scope systems beyond a VPN connection, an authorized IP address via a SSH public
key cryptographic connection is required for remote access to production infrastructure. For access to a server in
the production environment, users must authenticate to the bastion host, which is centrally managed via Chef, a
tool responsible for matching configurations across servers with recipes.
Additionally, the cloud platforms utilized in MongoDB’s in scope cloud products, which include AWS, Azure, and
GCP, are configured to authenticate users through SSO with a unique user account, minimum password
requirements, and MFA. Administrative functions on the server level require the MongoDB employee to
authenticate via a bastion with multi-factor authentication that includes a public key and user inserted verification
code. Administrative functionality at the infrastructure and cloud platform levels is restricted to authorized IT
personnel. To perform administrative tasks, MongoDB users utilize their individual accounts and do not use root
cloud accounts. These individual accounts have privileges that are commensurate with the user’s roles and
responsibilities.
Access Requests and Access Revocation
Documented policies and procedures are in place to guide personnel in the requirements for processing and
provisioning user access requests. Access requests are documented within a ticketing system and require manager
approval. MongoDB operates a multi-layered process, requiring multiple approvals in order to grant privileged
access to the MongoDB Cloud product environments (i.e., the CCP and the ACDP) to a very limited set of
individuals. Terminations are handled by a predefined group of users in the access management system (MANA).
One individual requests the termination and another approves before the information is sent to MANA from the HR
system. Predefined groups are utilized to assign role-based access privileges and segregate access to data
maintained within the application system.
Access revocation begins when HR enters a request for termination within the HR system and an automated e-mail
notifies IT personnel that a user will be terminated. After the automated e-mail notification is sent, an automated
script initiates the removal and deactivation of the user’s access to the systems. If an error occurs in the termination
process an automated e-mail notification is sent that requests further investigation. The IT team will investigate
and remove the access (disabling where necessary). User access reviews, including privileged user accounts, are
performed on at least a quarterly basis to help ensure that access to data is restricted to authorized personnel.
System Monitoring
Firewalls are utilized to block unauthorized inbound network traffic from the Internet. Firewalls are configured to
deny any type of network connection that is not explicitly authorized by a firewall rule. Additionally, firewalls are
configured to log access related events and send an e-mail alert to operations personnel when predefined events
occur (such as attempted unauthorized access or distributed denial of service (DDOS) attacks). Cloud engineering
and cloud security team members are responsible for researching the cause of the alert and taking actions as
deemed necessary.
To help identify potential security vulnerabilities on the production network, security management performs network
vulnerability scans on a daily basis. In addition, a qualified third party conducts a penetration test at least once per
calendar year.

13
This document was distributed using Conveyor, a secure customer trust management platform. For information about how
you can start using Conveyor for free to build trust with your customers, visit www.conveyor.com.

Privileged user access events and activity in the cloud service provider administrator consoles (AWS, GCP, and
Azure), including root cloud accounts, along with cloud API calls, are monitored through cloud native audit logs
which are configured to be analyzed by a centralized security information and event management (SIEM) tool.
Alerts are automatically sent via e-mail to SREs and cloud security personnel when predefined events occur and
perform research and take appropriate action as deemed necessary. In addition, security alerts on critical
infrastructure modifications are enabled and generated via the aforementioned SIEM solution. Any suspicious
activity is escalated to cloud engineering and security teams for further investigation.
Incident Response
Documented escalation procedures for reporting security incidents are provided to internal and external users to
guide users in identifying and reporting failures, incidents, concerns, and other complaints. The incident handling
process includes a six step PICERL (Prepare, Identify, Contain, Eradicate, Recover, Learn) process for addressing
information security incidents. MongoDB utilizes this process to ensure lessons learned are adopted and fed back
into preparation cycles. IT operations personnel utilize a ticketing system to document security incidents,
responses, and resolution. Once an incident is identified, a security incident ticket is opened and classified based
on the threat level of the reported incident. The Security Incident will be categorized into the highest applicable
level of one or more of the following categories:
•

Severity One – security incident involves customer data.

•

Severity Two – security incident that could, but is unlikely to, involve personal information or have a
business impact.

•

Severity Three – routine event that is unlikely to impact business functions and does not involve personal
information.

The response team evaluates the threat and track resolution progress within the ticket until remediation. Incidents
requiring a change to the system follow the standard change control process. For Severity 1 Incidents, the Security
Incident Task Force will convene to evaluate and understand the nature and cause of the security incident.
Change Management
MongoDB’s change control policies and procedures define the change management process that governs the way
software and infrastructure changes, including configuration changes, product development, and security patching,
are introduced into production environments, and how such changes are communicated to various stakeholders.
A ticketing system is in place to centrally maintain, manage, and monitor change requests. An automated
monitoring tool is configured to run a scan of the repositories for all commits to the master branch to ensure that all
commits met approval and testing requirements on a daily basis and sends a notification to cloud engineering
personnel if any commit was merged without meeting appropriate requirements. A file integrity monitoring tool is
also in place to alert cloud engineering (including security) personnel of any changes that have been moved into
production. Cloud Engineering is responsible for reviewing the alerts and confirming that the implemented changes
properly tie back to noted changes within the ticketing system that have properly followed the established change
lifecycle.
Cloud engineering personnel and executive management also participate in a change management meeting on a
semi-weekly basis to discuss security of MongoDB Cloud Services Platform environment and the business impact
of potential changes to the system. Each change must be discussed, prioritized, and approved during this meeting
in order to be implemented. Additionally, Cloud Engineering management reviews major release changes to inscope systems on a quarterly basis. The ability to implement changes is restricted to user accounts accessible by
authorized cloud engineering personnel and the production environment is logically and physically segmented from
the development and test environments. Management and engineers are notified of changes and ongoing and
upcoming projects that affect the in-scope systems via the monthly change management prioritization meetings.
Data Backup and Disaster Recovery
MongoDB utilizes an automated backup system for the databases within the cloud platforms to perform at least
daily scheduled backups of production data. Additionally, cloud services personnel perform restoration of backup
files as a component of business operations on at least an annual basis. In the event of a failure of a backup, the
backup tools are configured to automatically notify cloud operations personnel via a centralized communication tool.
Site reliability engineers are responsible for performing required follow-up on the backup failure and taking steps as
14
This document was distributed using Conveyor, a secure customer trust management platform. For information about how
you can start using Conveyor for free to build trust with your customers, visit www.conveyor.com.

deemed necessary. AWS, GCP, and Azure replication tools to automatically replicate critical data backups across
geographically different regions on at least a monthly basis.
A business continuity plan is in place to guide personnel in the event of a physical, environmental, or system disaster
and is reviewed and updated by executive management on a semi-annual basis. The business continuity plan is
reviewed, tested, and updated on at least a semi-annual basis. As a component of the business continuity test,
backup file restoration is performed to ensure backup systems are functioning as intended.
Vendor Management
To address risks associated with vendors, management has documented and maintains a vendor security policy
which provides guidelines for managing risk during vendor onboarding and ongoing reassessment due diligence
procedures. Contracts are required to be in place with vendors to communicate security commitments and establish
base level requirements for services purchased. Monitoring procedures are in place to help ensure continual
adherence to contractual agreements by vendors and business partners is occurring as expected. To help ensure
that this level of due diligence and monitoring takes place, management formally reviews vendors on an annual
basis through questionnaires, obtaining independent assessment reports over vendors, or a combination thereof.
As part of this review management considers changes to their vendors, the overall performance of their obligations,
and the organization’s objectives to determine if a continued relationship is beneficial.
Data
MongoDB stores infrastructure data, such as access logs, firewall logs, application logs, error logs, and cloud
infrastructure API logs, including authentication logs which allow for MongoDB personnel to perform investigative
research, as deemed necessary, and take action based on information contained within the data of the logs.
Customer data is encrypted and is not available to MongoDB personnel. Customers are responsible for the deletion
of their own data upon the end of an engagement.

CONTROL ENVIRONMENT
The control environment at MongoDB is the foundation for the other areas of internal control. It sets the tone of the
organization and influences the control consciousness of its personnel. The components of the control environment
factors include the integrity and ethical values; management’s commitment to competence; its organizational
structure; the assignment of authority and responsibility; and the oversight and direction provided by the board of
directors and operations management and operations management.
The control environment at MongoDB is the foundation for the other areas of internal control. It sets the tone of the
organization and influences the control consciousness of its personnel. The components of the control environment
factors include the integrity and ethical values, management’s commitment to competence; its organizational
structure; the assignment of authority and responsibility; and the oversight and direction provided by the board of
directors and operations management.
Integrity and Ethical Values
The effectiveness of controls cannot rise above the integrity and ethical values of the people who create, administer,
and monitor them. Integrity and ethical values are essential elements of MongoDB’s control environment, affecting
the design, administration, and monitoring of other components. Integrity and ethical behavior are the product of
MongoDB’s ethical and behavioral standards, how they are communicated, and how they are reinforced in
16
This document was distributed using Conveyor, a secure customer trust management platform. For information about how
you can start using Conveyor for free to build trust with your customers, visit www.conveyor.com.

practices. They include management’s actions to remove or reduce incentives and temptations that might prompt
personnel to engage in dishonest, illegal, or unethical acts. They also include the communication of entity values
and behavioral standards to personnel through policy statements and codes of conduct. Specific control activities
that MongoDB has implemented in this area are described below:
•

Organizational policy statements and employee handbook, containing a code of conduct, are documented
and communicate entity values and behavioral standards to which employees are required to adhere.

•

Employees sign an acknowledgment form indicating that they have been given access to the organizational
policies and codes of conduct and understand their responsibility for adhering to the associated values,
policies, procedures, and behavioral standards.

•

Employees sign an employment agreement containing a confidentiality statement agreeing not to disclose
proprietary or confidential information, including customer information, to unauthorized parties.

•

Background checks are performed for employees as a component of the hiring process.

Board of Directors Oversight
The oversight responsibilities of the board of directors are essential to the continued functioning of internal controls.
The board of directors is required to evaluate the expertise required among its members to determine the skills best
suited to determine the performance of a control and development of controls. Specific control activities that
MongoDB has implemented in this area are described below:
•

A board of directors is in place to oversee management activities.

•

The board of directors meets quarterly to discuss management activities and operational issues.

•

The board is empowered to create committees relating to key areas of their internal control responsibilities,
i.e., audit and security.

•

Board members attest to their independence.

Organizational Structure and Assignment of Authority and Responsibility
MongoDB’s organizational structure provides the framework within which its activities for achieving entity-wide
objectives are planned, executed, controlled, and monitored. MongoDB’s management believes that establishing
a relevant organizational structure includes considering key areas of authority and responsibility and established
lines of reporting. MongoDB has developed an organizational structure suited to its needs. This organizational
structure is based, in part, on its size and the nature of its activities.
MongoDB’s assignment of authority and responsibility activities include factors such as how authority and
responsibility for operating activities are assigned and how reporting relationships and authorization hierarchies are
established. It also includes policies relating to business practices, knowledge and experience of key personnel,
and resources provided for carrying out duties. In addition, it includes policies and communications directed at
helping ensure that personnel understand the entity’s objectives, know how their individual actions interrelate and
contribute to those objectives, and recognize how and for what they will be held accountable. Organizational charts
are in place to communicate key areas of authority, responsibility, and established lines of reporting to personnel.
These charts are communicated to employees and updated as needed.
Individuals are made clearly aware of their respective roles in the control environment through the use of
documented job descriptions and established reporting structures.
Commitment to Competence
MongoDB management defines competence as the knowledge and skills necessary to accomplish tasks that define
employee’s roles and responsibilities.
MongoDB’s commitment to competence includes management’s
consideration of the competence levels for particular jobs and how those levels translate into requisite skills and
knowledge.

Accountability
MongoDB’s management philosophy and operating style encompasses a broad range of characteristics. Such
characteristics include management’s approach to taking and monitoring business risks, and management’s
attitudes toward information processing, accounting functions and personnel.

RISK ASSESSMENT
Objective Setting
MongoDB specifies objectives with sufficient clarity to enable the identification and assessment of risks related to
objectives. Key members of the executive management, Governance, Risk and Compliance (GRC), information
security, and operational teams meet on an ongoing basis to identify and review business objectives. The
identification and assessment of risks related to business objectives is an integral part of the MongoDB risk
assessment process.
Risk Identification and Analysis
Management is responsible for identifying risks that threaten achievement of the control activities stated in the
management’s description of the services organizations systems. Management has implemented a process for
identifying relevant risks that could affect the organization’s ability to provide reliable service to its user entities.
This process includes estimating the significance of identified risks, assessing the likelihood of their occurrence,
and deciding about actions to address them. Key members of the executive management, GRC, and operational
teams meet on an annual basis to identify and review risks to the system. These risks are documented in a formal
report and individually tracked in the Jira ticketing system and used for the risk analysis and remediation plan stages
of the assessment.
Risk analysis is an essential process to the entity’s success. It includes identification of key business processes
where potential exposures of some consequence exist, as well as significant changes to those processes. Once
the significance and likelihood of risk have been assessed, management considers how the risk should be
managed. This involves judgment based on assumptions about the risk, and reasonable analysis of costs
associated with reducing the level of risk. Necessary actions are taken to reduce the significance or likelihood of
the risk occurring, and identification of the control activities necessary to mitigate the risk. Management has
identified these control activities and documented them in the Trust Services Criteria and Related Control Activities
section below. Additionally, management reviews the assessed risk levels on an annual basis and documents the
risk assessment in the annual risk program.
Risk Factors
Management considers risks that can arise from both external and internal factors including the following:
External Factors
•

Technological developments
18
This document was distributed using Conveyor, a secure customer trust management platform. For information about how
you can start using Conveyor for free to build trust with your customers, visit www.conveyor.com.

•

Changing customer needs or expectations

•

Competition that could alter marketing or service activities

•

New legislation and regulation that could force changes in policies and strategies

•

Natural catastrophes that could lead to changes in operations or information systems

•

Economic changes that could have an impact on management decisions

Internal Factors
•

Significant changes in policies, processes, or personnel

•

Types of fraud

•

Fraud incentives and pressures for employees

•

Fraud opportunities

•

Employee attitudes and rationalizations for fraud

•

A disruption in information systems processing

•

The quality of personnel hired, and methods of training utilized

•

Changes in management responsibilities

Potential for Fraud
MongoDB considers the potential for fraud in assessing risks to the archive of business objectives. During the
annual risk assessment, MongoDB identifies opportunities, pressures, incentives, and rationalizations that may lead
to the potential for fraud. Risks identified during this process are assessed and mitigated during the regular risk
assessment process.
Risk Remediation
Once risks have been identified and analyzed, the results are reviewed with leadership for appropriateness and
accuracy against the risk tolerance criteria. Leadership will then decide how to address risks within the various
ranges. Risk mitigation options include tolerate, treat, transfer, and terminate. If the determination is to treat the
risk, there is an associated control selected which is then associated with the Statement of Applicability. Risks are
then re-evaluated to determine residual risk and the residual risk score. Risk owners must implement risk treatment
plans for residual risk scores over defined thresholds.

TRUST SERVICES CRITERIA, HITRUST CSF CRITERIA, AND RELATED
CONTROL ACTIVITIES
Integration with Risk Assessment
Along with assessing risks, management has identified and put into effect actions needed to address those risks.
In order to address risks, control activities have been placed into operation to help ensure that the actions are
carried out properly and efficiently. Control activities serve as mechanisms for managing the achievement of the
security, availability, and confidentiality categories and the associated HITRUST CSF criteria.

INFORMATION AND COMMUNICATION SYSTEMS
Pertinent information must be identified, captured, and communicated in a form and timeframe that enables people
to carry out their responsibilities. Information systems produce reports containing operational, financial, and
compliance-related information, that make it possible to run and control the business. They deal not only with
internally generated data, but also information about external events, activities, and conditions necessary to inform
business decision-making and external reporting. Effective communication also must occur in a broader sense,
flowing down, across and up the organization. Personnel must receive a clear message from top management that
control responsibilities must be taken seriously. They must understand their own role in the internal control system,
as well as how individual activities relate to the work of others. They must have a means of communicating
significant information upstream. There also needs to be effective communication with external parties, such as
customers, suppliers, regulators, and shareholders.
Internal Communications
MongoDB has implemented various methods of communication to help provide assurance that employees
understand their individual roles and responsibilities and that significant events are communicated. These methods
include orientation for new employees, training for each employee, and the use of e-mail and instant messaging
applications to communicate time-sensitive information. Employees are encouraged to communicate to their
manager or executive management.

If incidents are identified, personnel communicate and follow documented incident response plan. For example, if
a change in procedure is required, the manager is advised of the change. Formal procedure changes are distributed
to management before they are incorporated into the policy and distributed to relevant parties. Incidents are
documented within the automated ticketing system and tracked by management until resolved.
External Communications
MongoDB has also implemented various methods of communication to help provide assurance that customers
understand the roles and responsibilities in processing their transactions and communication of significant events.
These methods include regular meetings with representatives from each customer, ability to report security and
vulnerability concerns to technical personnel, and the use of e-mail messages and the customer contact line to
communicate time-sensitive information.

MONITORING
Monitoring is a process that assesses the quality of internal control performance over time. It involves assessing
the design and operation of controls and taking necessary corrective actions. This process is accomplished through
ongoing activities, separate evaluation, or a combination of the two. Monitoring activities also include using
information from communications from external parties such as user entity complaints and regulatory comments
that may indicate problems or highlight areas in need of improvement. Management has implemented a selfassessment and compliance program to ensure the controls are consistently applied as designed.
Ongoing Monitoring
Examples of MongoDB’s ongoing monitoring activities include the following:
•

Changes to the in-scope MongoDB Cloud Services Platform products’ source code or configuration
parameters are monitored by the file integrity monitoring tool.

•

At least annually, the security team reviews system architecture, configuration, security, and components
as they relate to latest industry standards, regulations, and technological capabilities. Any changes based
on this review are triaged and tracked to resolution by the security oversight team.

•

In carrying out its regular management activities, operating management obtains evidence that the system
of internal control continues to function.

•

Communications from external parties and customers corroborate internally generated information or
indicate problems.

•

Organizational structure and supervisory activities provide oversight of control functions and identification
of deficiencies.

•

Planning sessions and other meetings provide important feedback to management on whether controls are
effective.

•

Personnel are briefed on organizational policy statements and codes of conduct to communicate entity
values.

•

Access to the in-scope MongoDB Cloud Services Platform products’ files, and stored assets, such as those
files stored in AWS, GCP, or Azure or those access points to the cloud platforms are monitored by the cloud
provider logs and reviewed on a periodic basis.

•

Personnel are briefed on organizational policy statements and codes of conduct to communicate entity
values.

•

MongoDB engages a qualified third-party to conduct an annual penetration testing and quarterly
vulnerability assessments as a component of their commitment to ongoing monitoring of the MongoDB
Cloud Services Platform environments. The findings of the annual testing and quarterly assessments are
discussed by management and the security team and actions are taken as deemed necessary based on
the findings of the reports.

•

MongoDB also performs an annual formal risk assessment over MongoDB Cloud Services Platform
environments and supporting business units and infrastructure. The findings of the annual risk assessment
are discussed by management, GRC, and the security oversight teams, and actions are taken, as deemed
necessary, based on the findings of the assessment.

Separate Evaluations
A number of reasons may prompt evaluation of an entire internal control system: major strategy or management
change, major acquisitions or dispositions, or significant changes in operations or methods of processing financial
information. Evaluations of internal control vary in scope and frequency, depending on the significance of risks
being controlled and the importance of the controls in reducing the risks. Controls addressing higher-priority risks
and those most essential to reducing a given risk will tend to be evaluated more often.
Often, evaluations take the form of self-assessments, where persons responsible for a particular unit or function will
determine the effectiveness of controls for their activities and relay them to management of the company.
Management, the GRC, and the security oversight teams consider these assessments, along with any other internal
control evaluations. The findings of these efforts are utilized to ensure follow-up actions are taken and subsequent
evaluations are modified, as necessary.
Subservice Organization Monitoring
The GRC team reviews the AWS, GCP, and Azure Type 2 SOC 2 reports, PCI Attestation of Compliance (AoCs)
and responsibilities matrices, ISO27001 and ISO 22301 accredited registrations on, at least, an annual and as
needed basis to ensure the design and operating effectiveness of controls at the subservice organization. Any
findings within the third-party reports are reviewed to determine impact and overall risk to MongoDB’s use of their
services with follow-up as necessary both internally and with the third-party provider.
System Incident Disclosures
No system incidents occurred that were the result of controls that were not suitably designed or otherwise resulted
in a significant failure of the achievement of one or more of the service commitments and systems requirements.
Evaluating and Communicating Deficiencies
Deficiencies in management’s internal control system surface from many sources, including the company’s ongoing
monitoring procedures, separate evaluations of the internal control system and external parties. Management and
the security oversight team have developed protocols to help ensure findings of internal control deficiencies are
reported not only to the individual responsible for the function or activity involved, who is in the position to take
corrective action, but also to at least one level of management above the directly responsible person. This process
enables that individual to provide needed support or oversight for taking corrective action, and to communicate with
others in the organization whose activities may be affected. Management and the security oversight team evaluates
the specific facts and circumstances related to deficiencies in internal control procedures and make the decision for
addressing deficiencies based on whether the incident was isolated or requires a change in the company’s
procedures or personnel.

COMPLEMENTARY CONTROLS AT USER ENTITIES
MongoDB’s controls are designed to provide reasonable assurance that the principal service commitments and
system requirements can be achieved without the implementation of complementary controls at user entities. As a
result, complementary user entity controls are not required, or significant, to achieve the principal service
commitments and system requirements based on the applicable trust services criteria.

22
This document was distributed using Conveyor, a secure customer trust management platform. For information about how
you can start using Conveyor for free to build trust with your customers, visit www.conveyor.com.

COMPLEMENTARY CONTROL RESPONSIBILITIES AT USER ENTITIES
As stated in the previous section, MongoDB’s controls are designed to provide reasonable assurance that the
principal service commitments and system requirements can be achieved without the implementation of
complementary controls at user entities. As a result, complementary user entity controls are not required, or
significant, to achieve the principal service commitments and system requirements based on the applicable trust
services criteria.
Under the shared responsibility model, certain aspects of security, confidentiality, and availability are explicitly
designated as the customer’s responsibility. The shared responsibility model is predicated on both parties fulfilling
their respective obligations; failure by the customer to implement their required responsibilities introduces risks that
are outside MongoDB’s control and may compromise the protection and availability of the customer’s data and
services.

TESTS OF OPERATING EFFECTIVENESS AND RESULTS OF TESTS
Scope of Testing
This report on the controls relates to the MongoDB Cloud Service Platform system provided by MongoDB. The
scope of the testing was restricted to the MongoDB Cloud Service Platform system and its boundaries as defined
in Section 3. Schellman conducted the examination testing over the period October 1, 2024, to March 31, 2025.
Tests of Operating Effectiveness
The tests applied to test the operating effectiveness of controls are listed alongside each of the respective control
activities within the Testing Matrices. Such tests were considered necessary to evaluate whether the controls were
sufficient to provide reasonable, but not absolute, assurance that the applicable trust services criteria and HITRUST
CSF criteria were achieved during the review period. In selecting the tests of controls, Schellman considered
various factors including, but not limited to, the following:
•

the nature of the control and the frequency with which it operates;

•

the control risk mitigated by the control;

•

the effectiveness of entity-level controls, especially controls that monitor other controls;

•

the degree to which the control relies on the effectiveness of other controls; and

•

whether the control is manually performed or automated.

The types of tests performed with respect to the operational effectiveness of the control activities detailed in this
section are briefly described below:
Test Approach

Description

Inquiry

Inquired of relevant personnel with the requisite knowledge and experience regarding
the performance and application of the related control activity. This included in-person
interviews, telephone calls, e-mails, web-based conferences, or a combination of the
preceding.

Observation

Observed the relevant processes or procedures during fieldwork. This included, but
was not limited to, witnessing the performance of controls or evidence of control
performance with relevant personnel, systems, or locations relevant to the
performance of control policies and procedures.

Inspection

Inspected the relevant audit records. This included, but was not limited to, documents,
system configurations and settings, or the existence of sampling attributes, such as
signatures, approvals, or logged events. In some cases, inspection testing involved
tracing events forward to consequent system documentation or processes (e.g.,
resolution, detailed documentation, alarms, etc.) or vouching backwards for
prerequisite events (e.g., approvals, authorizations, etc.).

Sampling
Consistent with American Institute of Certified Public Accountants (AICPA) authoritative literature, Schellman
utilizes professional judgment to consider the tolerable deviation rate, the expected deviation rate, the audit risk,
the characteristics of the population, and other factors, in order to determine the number of items to be selected in
a sample for a particular test. Schellman, in accordance with AICPA authoritative literature, selected samples in
such a way that the samples were expected to be representative of the population. This included judgmental
selection methods, where applicable, to ensure representative samples were obtained.

25
This document was distributed using Conveyor, a secure customer trust management platform. For information about how
you can start using Conveyor for free to build trust with your customers, visit www.conveyor.com.

System-generated population listings were obtained whenever possible to ensure completeness prior to selecting
samples. In some instances, full populations were tested in cases including but not limited to, the uniqueness of
the event or low overall population size.
Reliability of Information Provided by the Service Organization
Observation and inspection procedures were performed related to certain system-generated reports, listings, and
queries to assess the accuracy and completeness (reliability) of the information used in the performance of our
testing of the controls.
Test Results
The results of each test applied are listed alongside each respective test applied within the Testing Matrices. Test
results not deemed as control deviations are noted by the phrase “No exceptions noted.” in the test result column
of the Testing Matrices. Any phrase other than the aforementioned, constitutes either a test result that is the result
of non-occurrence, a change in the application of the control activity, or a deficiency in the operating effectiveness
of the control activity. Testing deviations identified within the Testing Matrices are not necessarily weaknesses in
the total system of controls, as this determination can only be made after consideration of controls in place at user
entities and subservice organizations, if applicable, and other factors. Control considerations that should be
implemented by subservice organizations, in order to complement the control activities and achieve the applicable
trust services criteria are presented in the “Subservice Organizations” section within Section 3.

Control Activities
CC5.1 – COSO Principle 10: The entity selects and develops control activities that contribute to the mitigation of risks to the
achievement of objectives to acceptable levels.
CC5.1.1

Security stakeholders perform a
risk assessment on an annual
basis that includes an analysis of
risk mitigation control activities.
The analysis considers how the
environment, complexity, nature,
and scope of its operations, as
well as the specific characteristics
of its organization, affect the
selection and development of
control activities.

Inspected the risk assessment
policy and procedures as well as
the most recently completed risk
assessment, risk register, and
mitigation plans to determine that
security stakeholders performed a
risk assessment that included an
analysis of risk mitigation control
activities and the analysis
considered how the environment,
complexity, nature, and scope of
its operations, as well as the
specific characteristics of its
organization, affected the
selection and development of
control activities during the period.

No exceptions noted.

CC5.1.2

Assigned risk owners select and
develop control activities to
mitigate the risks identified during
the annual risk assessment
process. The control activities are
documented within the mitigation
plans that are created by the risk
owners for risks above the
tolerable threshold.

Inspected the most recently
completed risk assessment, risk
register, and mitigation plans to
determine that assigned risk
owners selected and developed
control activities to mitigate the
risks identified during the annual
risk assessment process and the
control activities were
documented within the mitigation
plans that were created by the risk
owners for risks above the
tolerable threshold during the
period.

No exceptions noted.

10.l - Outsourced Software Development: Outsourced software development shall be supervised and monitored by the
organization.
Not applicable. MongoDB does not outsource software development.
10.m - Control of Technical Vulnerabilities: Timely information about technical vulnerabilities of information systems being
used shall be obtained; the organization's exposure to such vulnerabilities evaluated; and appropriate measures taken to
address the associated risk.
10.m.1

Internal vulnerability scans of the
production systems are
configured to run on a daily basis
and to send an alert to
management of identified threats.

Inspected the internal vulnerability
scan and alert configuration and
an example alert generated during
the period to determine that
internal vulnerability scans of the
production systems were
configured to run on a daily basis
and to send an alert to
management of identified threats.

No exceptions noted.

10.m.2

Security operations and
infrastructure teams track, review,
and remediate security
vulnerabilities identified in the
vulnerability scans and
penetration tests according to the
security remediation standards.

Inspected the vulnerability
dashboard and an example ticket
generated during the period to
determine that security operations
and infrastructure teams tracked,
reviewed, and remediated security
vulnerabilities identified in the
vulnerability scans and
penetration tests according to the
security remediation standards.

No exceptions noted.

10.m.3

Security and help desk personnel
utilize a ticketing system in order
to track, review, and remediate
incidents.

Inspected the incident ticketing
system dashboard and a sample
of incidents remediated during the
period to determine that security
and help desk personnel utilized a
ticketing system to track, review,
and remediate incidents for each
incident sampled.

No exceptions noted.

11.a - Reporting Information Security Events: Information security events shall be reported through appropriate
communications channels as quickly as possible. All employees, contractors and third-party users shall be made aware of
their responsibility to report any information security events as quickly as possible.
11.a.1

Documented escalation policies
and procedures for reporting
security incidents are provided to
internal users to guide users in
identifying and reporting failures,
incidents, concerns, and other
complaints.

Inspected evidence of internal
escalation policies and
procedures to determine that
documented escalation policies
and procedures for reporting
security incidents were provided
to internal users to guide users in
identifying and reporting failures,
incidents, concerns, and other
complaints.

No exceptions noted.

12.b - Business Continuity and Risk Assessment: Events that can cause interruptions to business processes shall be
identified, along with the probability and impact of such interruptions and their consequences for information security.
12.b.1

A business continuity plan is in
place to guide personnel in the
event of a physical,
environmental, or system disaster
and is reviewed and updated by
executive management on at least
a semi-annual basis.

Inspected the business continuity
plan and revision history to
determine that a business
continuity plan was in place to
guide personnel in the event of a
physical, environmental, or
system disaster and executive
management reviewed and
updated the plan during the
period.

No exceptions noted.
